usage: be careful in the heat wave
examples: 요즘 폭염 때문에 밖에 나가기가 힘들어요.
Because of the heat wave these days it is hard to go outside.
오늘 폭염 경보가 내려서 야외 활동을 자제하래요.
A heat wave warning was issued today so they say to refrain from outdoor activity.
In a heat wave you have to drink water often.
nuance: 폭염 is the formal word you hear on the news and in phone alerts for an extreme summer heat wave, stronger than the everyday 더위. From late July Koreans get 폭염 경보 push alerts on their phones, so recognizing this word matters for daily life.
mistakes: Confusing 폭염 (heat wave) with the casual 더위 (heat) and using it in light small talk
Saying 폭염이 와요 instead of the natural 폭염이 계속돼요 or 폭염이 심해요

usage: a cold wave is sweeping in
examples: 이번 주에 한파가 와서 정말 추워요.
A cold wave came this week so it is really cold.
Because of the cold wave the water pipes froze.
한파가 올 때는 외출을 줄이는 게 좋아요.
When a cold wave comes it is better to go out less.
nuance: 한파 is the winter counterpart of 폭염, used on the news and in phone alerts for a sudden severe cold snap. Unlike the everyday 추위, 한파 implies a sharp, warning-level drop in temperature that can freeze pipes and disrupt daily life.
mistakes: Using 한파 for ordinary cold weather when plain 추워요 is enough
Saying 한파가 내려요 instead of the natural 한파가 와요 or 한파가 닥쳐요

examples: 오늘 황사가 심해서 마스크를 꼭 써야 해요.
The yellow dust is severe today so you really have to wear a mask.
Every spring the yellow dust blows in from China.
Because of the yellow dust I cannot open the windows.
nuance: 황사 is the seasonal sand-and-dust haze that blows in from the deserts of China and Mongolia, peaking in spring. It is distinct from 미세먼지 (fine dust): 황사 is coarse desert sand, while 미세먼지 is fine particulate pollution, though news reports often mention them together.
mistakes: Treating 황사 and 미세먼지 as the same thing when they are different phenomena
Saying 황사가 와요 in formal speech where 황사가 심해요 or 황사가 불어와요 sounds more natural

usage: I got caught in a shower
examples: A sudden shower fell out of nowhere so I got all wet.
In summer sudden showers often come in the afternoon.
A sudden shower stops quickly so just wait a moment.
nuance: 소나기 is a brief, intense shower that comes and goes suddenly, very common on summer afternoons in Korea. Unlike steady 비, a 소나기 is short-lived, so people often just wait it out under a roof instead of buying an umbrella.
mistakes: Using 소나기 for long, steady rain when it specifically means a brief sudden burst
Forgetting that 소나기 uses 내리다 or 오다, not a special verb

examples: 밤에 천둥이 쳐서 잠을 못 잤어요.
Thunder struck at night so I could not sleep.
The sound of thunder was so loud that I was startled.
천둥이 칠 때는 우산보다 건물 안이 안전해요.
When thunder strikes a building is safer than an umbrella.
nuance: 천둥 is the sound of thunder and pairs with the verb 치다, as in 천둥이 쳐요. Koreans almost always say it together with 번개 as the set phrase 천둥 번개 when describing a storm.
mistakes: Saying 천둥이 와요 instead of the correct 천둥이 쳐요
Mixing up 천둥 (the sound, thunder) with 번개 (the flash, lightning)

examples: Lightning flashed outside the window so it was scary.
천둥 번개가 칠 때는 밖에 나가지 마세요.
When there is thunder and lightning do not go outside.
After the lightning strikes you hear the thunder.
nuance: 번개 is the flash of lightning and, like 천둥, takes the verb 치다. In casual speech 번개 also means a spontaneous last-minute meetup (번개 모임), so context decides whether it is weather or a quick get-together.
mistakes: Confusing 번개 (the flash, lightning) with 천둥 (the sound, thunder)
Saying 번개가 와요 instead of the natural 번개가 쳐요

examples: Frost fell at dawn so the grass is white.
The first frost has already fallen.
On a day with frost the road is slippery.
nuance: 서리 is the thin white frost that forms on cold autumn and early-winter mornings, and it pairs with the verb 내리다. The 첫서리 (first frost) is a small seasonal marker Koreans mention when the weather turns sharply colder.
mistakes: Confusing 서리 (frost) with 얼음 (ice) or 눈 (snow)
Saying 서리가 와요 instead of the natural 서리가 내려요

usage: roads are blocked by heavy snow
examples: Roads were all blocked by last night's heavy snow.
Heavy snow fell so the flight was canceled.
When heavy snow comes use public transportation.
nuance: 폭설 is heavy, disruptive snowfall and the snow counterpart of 폭우, often paired with 경보 in weather alerts. It signals snow heavy enough to block roads and cancel transit, unlike the neutral 눈 used for ordinary snow.
mistakes: Using 폭설 for light, pretty snowfall when plain 눈 fits better
Saying 폭설이 와요 stiffly where 폭설이 내려요 sounds more natural in writing

usage: the daily temperature range is big
the day-night temperature gap is severe
a cold from the temperature gap
examples: 요즘 일교차가 커서 감기에 걸리기 쉬워요.
The daily temperature range is big these days so it is easy to catch a cold.
In spring and autumn the day-night temperature gap is severe.
Since the temperature swing is big bring an outer layer.
nuance: 일교차 is the gap between the day's high and low temperature, a phrase Koreans use constantly in spring and autumn weather reports. It is described with 크다 (big) or 심하다 (severe), and is almost always linked to advice about layering clothes or catching a cold.
mistakes: Describing 일교차 with 높다/낮다 instead of the correct 크다/작다
Confusing 일교차 (day-night gap) with 기온 (the temperature itself)

usage: can't sleep because of the tropical night
examples: 열대야 때문에 밤에 잠을 못 자요.
Because of the tropical night I cannot sleep at night.
요즘 열대야가 계속돼서 에어컨을 켜고 자요.
Tropical nights continue these days so I sleep with the air conditioner on.
On a night of severe tropical heat it is hot even at dawn.
nuance: 열대야 refers to a sweltering summer night when the temperature stays above 25 degrees and does not cool down, making sleep difficult. It is a staple of Korean summer news and small talk, almost always tied to complaints about not sleeping and running the air conditioner.
mistakes: Using 열대야 for any hot day rather than specifically a hot, sleepless night
Misspelling it as 열대얄 or 열데야 instead of 열대야

examples: In summer the humidity is high so it feels hotter.
When the humidity is low laundry dries quickly.
장마철에는 습도 때문에 곰팡이가 잘 생겨요.
During the rainy season mold forms easily because of the humidity.
nuance: 습도 is humidity and, unlike most weather words, it takes 높다 (high) and 낮다 (low) rather than 크다 or 오다. Koreans bring it up constantly in muggy summers to explain why the heat feels worse, and it ties into talk of mold, laundry, and dehumidifiers.
mistakes: Saying 습도가 많아요 instead of the correct 습도가 높아요
Confusing 습도 (humidity) with 온도 (temperature)

examples: Heavy rain suddenly poured down so the road got flooded.
Because of the heavy rain the subway stopped.
폭우가 올 때는 지하 주차장을 조심하세요.
When heavy rain comes be careful of underground parking lots.
nuance: 폭우 is a torrential downpour serious enough to flood streets, stronger than ordinary 비 or a passing 소나기. It commonly takes the vivid verb 쏟아지다 (to pour down) and appears with 경보 in summer flood warnings, so it carries a sense of danger and disruption.
mistakes: Using 폭우 for ordinary or light rain when plain 비 is enough
Saying 폭우가 와요 flatly where 폭우가 쏟아져요 captures the intensity better
